findings.title: Any authenticated user can read destination plugin secrets (SFTP password, key passphrase, export passphrase) via GET /destinations
findings.impact: Every logged-in principal, including the lowest-privilege read-only user, can dump the stored credential values of every configured destination. For the SFTP destination that is the plaintext `password` and `privateKeyPass` of an account whose default user is root on the certificate-serving hosts; for other destination plugins it is the cloud account/API credentials, and for a nested export plugin it is the keystore/PEM passphrase. That is a direct privilege escalation from 'Lemur user' to 'shell on the destination servers' and to the material needed to decrypt exported private keys.
findings.evidence: DestinationsList.get (views.py:36-37), Destinations.get (views.py:198-199) and CertificateDestinations.get (views.py:360-361) are only decorated with @validate_schema and inherit AuthenticatedResource (login only). The mutating siblings on the same resources are explicitly gated: post (views.py:102), put (views.py:254) and delete (views.py:348) all carry @admin_permission.require(http_exception=403) -- the intent that destinations are admin-managed is stated in the file, and only the read path is missing it. The response body is not redacted: DestinationOutputSchema declares `options = fields.List(fields.Dict())` (schemas.py:28) and fill_object copies the raw option list into the plugin block (schemas.py:33) and expands nested export-plugin options (schemas.py:36). Option dicts carry their `value`, as the endpoint's own documented sample response shows (views.py:62-69, "value": "111111111111111"). The SFTP plugin's module docstring confirms the values are stored unencrypted: "Passwords are not encrypted and stored as a plain text" (lemur/plugins/lemur_sftp/plugin.py:13), and it registers `password` (plugin.py:63) and `privateKeyPass` (plugin.py:77) as ordinary str options.
findings.recommendation: Either gate the three GET handlers with @admin_permission.require(http_exception=403) like their write counterparts, or -- since the UI needs the destination list for certificate creation -- strip secrets in the output schema: flag sensitive plugin options in each plugin's option definitions (e.g. `"sensitive": True`) and have DestinationOutputSchema.fill_object replace their `value` with a mask unless admin_permission.can(). Encrypting the values at rest (Vault/KMS or Lemur's encrypted column type) should follow, so that a DB read is not equivalent to a credential dump.

findings.title: SFTP plugin chmods the uploaded TLS private key to 0644, world-readable on the destination host
findings.impact: Every private key Lemur delivers over SFTP is left world-readable on the target server. Any local account on that host -- a compromised low-privilege service, a shared-shell user, a container sharing the mount -- can read the key for the site's TLS certificate and use it to decrypt captured traffic or impersonate the service. The same line also widens the permissions of an ACME HTTP-01 token file, but the key is the real loss.
findings.evidence: upload() builds the file set as `files = {cn + ".key": private_key, cn + ".pem": body}` (plugin.py:155), i.e. the private key is one of the entries. upload_file() then applies the same permission to every entry with no discrimination: `sftp.chmod(path.join(dst_path, filename), 0o644)` (plugin.py:281), executed unconditionally after each write inside the `for filename, data in files.items()` loop (plugin.py:264). The in-line comment -- "most likely the upload user isn't the webuser, -rw-r--r--" (plugin.py:280) -- shows the mode was chosen for readability by the web server, without separating key material from public material. Note the permission-denied retry path uses 0o600 (plugin.py:277) and is then immediately overwritten by the 0o644 on line 281.
findings.recommendation: Set the mode per file rather than globally: keep 0644 for the certificate/chain/ACME token and use 0600 (or 0640 with an explicit group set via sftp.chown) for anything carrying private_key. Best is to make the mode a plugin option (e.g. `certFileMode`/`keyFileMode`, defaulting to 0644/0600) so operators whose web server runs as a different user can grant access via group instead of world. Also apply the mode before or immediately after creation rather than after the content is written, to avoid a window where the key exists with the server's default umask.

findings.title: Certificate common name is concatenated into the remote path, allowing directory traversal outside destinationPath on the SFTP host
findings.impact: A user who can get a certificate into Lemur with a chosen subject CN and attach an existing SFTP destination can make Lemur write attacker-supplied `.pem` and `.key` files -- and create directories -- anywhere on the remote filesystem the SFTP account can reach (default account is root, plugin.py:59-60). Concrete abuses: drop the key/cert pair into a web root so the private key is fetchable over HTTP (compounded by F-002's 0644), or overwrite another service's certificate and key pair with one the attacker controls, producing an outage or a serving-key swap. Directory creation and file overwrite happen with no confirmation.
findings.evidence: upload() derives the path from certificate content: `cn = common_name(parse_certificate(body))` (plugin.py:149) then `dst_path_cn = dst_path + "/" + cn` (plugin.py:151), a raw string concatenation with no normalisation, no check that the result stays under dst_path, and no rejection of `/` or `..` inside cn. The same untrusted cn is also used to build the file names (plugin.py:155, 160, 164), so both path components are attacker-influenced. upload_file() then walks the segments and creates every missing directory (plugin.py:234-261) before opening the file for write (plugin.py:269). Contrast the ACME paths, which do defend themselves by discarding the directory part -- `_, filename = path.split(token_path)` (plugin.py:175, 186) -- showing the sanitising idiom is known in this file but not applied to cn.
findings.recommendation: Treat cn as untrusted input. Reduce it to a single safe path component before use: reject or slugify anything matching `[/\\]` or `..`, reject an empty/None cn (common_name can return None, which currently raises TypeError on line 151 and is then swallowed by F-004), and after joining, assert `os.path.normpath(dst_path_cn).startswith(os.path.normpath(dst_path) + "/")`, aborting the upload otherwise. Applying the same check to each entry of `files` closes the second half of the traversal.

findings.title: upload_file swallows most exceptions, so a failed certificate delivery is reported to Lemur as a success
findings.impact: Any failure that is not an AuthenticationException, not a NoValidConnectionsError and does not carry an `.errors` attribute -- a rejected host key, a full disk, a permission error with an errno other than 13, a paramiko protocol error, a TypeError from a None common name -- is logged at error level and then discarded, and upload_file returns normally. The caller therefore records the destination as successfully provisioned while nothing was written. Operators lose the signal that certificate rotation stopped working, which surfaces later as an expired-certificate outage on the destination hosts.
findings.evidence: The outer handler catches everything (`except Exception as e`, plugin.py:287), logs, closes the session, and re-raises only inside `if hasattr(e, 'errors')` (plugin.py:294-298); there is no `raise` on the path where the attribute is absent. Inside the loop, the permission retry has the same shape: `except PermissionError as permerror: if permerror.errno == 13:` (plugin.py:271-272) with no else and no re-raise, so a non-13 permission error is silently absorbed and execution falls through to the chmod on line 281. delete_file has the identical structure (plugin.py:219-224), so a failed ACME token cleanup is also silent, leaving challenge tokens on the server. The `message` variable built at plugin.py:293-296 keeps only the last error of the loop, discarding the rest.
findings.recommendation: Re-raise unconditionally after logging: build the message when `e.errors` exists and fall back to `str(e)` otherwise, but raise in both branches so the destination plugin contract reports failure. In the permission retry, add an `else: raise` for errno values other than EACCES. Consider raising a dedicated plugin exception type so the caller can distinguish connection failures from write failures.

findings.title: NoValidConnectionsError is re-raised with a string argument, so the connection-failure handler itself throws AttributeError
findings.impact: Every genuine 'cannot reach the SFTP host' condition (timeout, refused port, bad hostname) is turned into an AttributeError raised from inside the except block, losing the original diagnostic. Because AttributeError is neither of the two types the callers re-raise and has no `.errors` attribute, it lands in the generic handler of F-004 and is swallowed -- so a total delivery outage is reported upstream as a successful upload. The two defects combine into silent, undetected non-delivery.
findings.evidence: plugin.py:142 does `raise NoValidConnectionsError("Couldn't connect to {0}, possible timeout or invalid hostname")`. paramiko's NoValidConnectionsError.__init__ expects a mapping of (address, port) -> error and immediately calls `errors.keys()` / sorts them, which raises AttributeError on a str. The callers catch `(AuthenticationException, NoValidConnectionsError)` and re-raise (plugin.py:217, 285), so they never see it; `except Exception` (plugin.py:287) does, and `hasattr(e, 'errors')` is False for AttributeError, so nothing is re-raised. The neighbouring line has a related defect: `raise AuthenticationException("Couldn't connect to {0}, due to an Authentication exception.")` (plugin.py:139) never formats `{0}`, so the message reaches the operator with a literal placeholder instead of the host.
findings.recommendation: Do not re-instantiate paramiko exception types with a message. Use bare `raise` to preserve the original exception and its context, or wrap it in a plugin-owned exception class carrying the formatted text (`raise SFTPConnectionError(f"Couldn't connect to {host}:{port}") from e`). Fix the unformatted `{0}` on line 139 at the same time, and update the callers' except tuple to the new type.

findings.title: RejectPolicy is set but no host keys are ever loaded, so every SFTP connection is rejected at host-key verification
findings.impact: paramiko's SSHClient starts with empty system and session host-key stores; nothing in this plugin populates them. With RejectPolicy installed, the missing-host-key branch fires on every connection and raises SSHException, so no certificate is ever delivered and no ACME HTTP-01 token is ever published through this plugin. It fails closed (no MITM exposure), but combined with F-004/F-005 the failure is invisible: uploads are reported successful while the destination is never touched, and ACME challenges fail at renewal time.
findings.evidence: `ssh = paramiko.SSHClient()` followed directly by `ssh.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.RejectPolicy())` (plugin.py:113-116); there is no `ssh.load_system_host_keys()` or `ssh.load_host_keys(...)` anywhere in the file, and no plugin option that would supply a known_hosts path or an expected fingerprint (option list, plugin.py:40-98). The comment immediately above the policy line still reads "allow connection to the new unknown host" (plugin.py:115), which describes AutoAddPolicy -- evidence that the policy was tightened without the rest of the change (loading known_hosts) being carried through.
findings.recommendation: Keep RejectPolicy and give it something to check against: call `ssh.load_system_host_keys()` plus `ssh.load_host_keys(path)` for an operator-supplied known_hosts file, exposed as a plugin option alongside host/port, or add an expected host-key fingerprint option verified against `transport.get_remote_server_key()`. Document the trust-on-first-use step for operators and update the stale comment on line 115.

findings.title: Unguarded dict access in DestinationOutputSchema.fill_object lets one malformed stored option 500 the whole destinations listing
findings.impact: A single destination row whose stored options do not match the shape assumed here breaks GET /destinations, GET /destinations/<id> and GET /certificates/<id>/destinations for every user, not just for that row -- the post_dump hook runs while serialising the list. That takes out the destination picker in the UI and any automation that enumerates destinations, until the offending row is repaired directly in the database.
findings.evidence: `if "export-plugin" in option["type"]` (schemas.py:35) indexes `type` without a default, raising KeyError for any option dict persisted without that key; the corresponding input path elsewhere in Lemur uses the defensive `option.get("type", "")` form. The next line, `option["value"]["pluginOptions"] = option["value"]["plugin_options"]` (schemas.py:36), assumes `value` is a dict holding `plugin_options`, so an export-plugin option whose value is null (never configured) or a plain string raises TypeError/KeyError. `data["plugin"]["pluginOptions"] = data["options"]` (schemas.py:33) likewise assumes the nested plugin dumped non-null. The stored options come from admin-supplied JSON (`data["plugin"]["plugin_options"]`, views.py:188 and 344), so the shape is not guaranteed by any column constraint. The membership test is also looser than intended: `"export-plugin" in option["type"]` is a substring match on the type string rather than an equality check.
findings.recommendation: Make the hook total: `for option in data.get("plugin", {}).get("pluginOptions", []) or []:` with `if option.get("type") == "export-plugin":` and a `isinstance(option.get("value"), dict) and "plugin_options" in option["value"]` guard before the copy. Validate option shape on input (name/type/value required) in DestinationInputSchema so malformed rows cannot be persisted in the first place.
